name: Buckingham Chainsaw Lanyard with Steel Ring
title: Buckingham Chainsaw Lanyard with Steel Ring
h1: Buckingham Chainsaw Lanyard with Steel Ring
meta: The Buckingham chainsaw lanyard with steel ring keeps your saw tethered to your saddle aloft. See how it rigs up, who it suits, and what it typically costs.
tagline: A stretchy saw tether with a steel ring end for climbers running a saw aloft.
summary: The Buckingham chainsaw lanyard with steel ring is a simple saw tether that keeps a top-handle or small rear-handle saw attached to your saddle while you work in the tree. The bungee body stretches when you reach for a cut and pulls the saw back in when you let it hang.
highlights: Bungee body stretches for reach and retracts when the saw hangs
Steel ring end for a solid connection on the saw or saddle side
Keeps a dropped saw off the ground crew
Fits most top-handle and small rear-handle saws
Simple, low-cost item worth keeping a spare of
specs: Tethering a saw to a climbing saddle

body.h: How it works on the climb
p: Most climbers clip the saw lanyard to a dedicated saw ring or side D on the saddle and attach the steel ring end to the saw's lanyard point, usually through a snap or a rated connector. When you pull the saw up to cut, the bungee stretches; when you let go, the saw hangs close to your hip instead of swinging around your legs.

The steel ring gives you a durable wear point. It does not wear through like a sewn loop on the bark-side of a saw, and it is easy to inspect. Keep the lanyard short enough that the saw cannot reach your legs or lanyard rope when it hangs.

Check the bungee for cuts, frayed sheath, and lost stretch, and replace it when it sags. Keep fuel and bar oil off the shock cord when you can. Browse other chainsaw lanyards if you want a hi-viz color, a coiled style, or a retractable reel.
A saw lanyard is not life support and is never a tie-in point. Run your saw to the manufacturer's instructions, wear your PPE, and follow ANSI Z133 for aloft saw work.

faq.q: Where do I clip a chainsaw lanyard on my saddle?
faq.a: Use the saw attachment point or side ring the saddle maker designates for tools. Never clip a saw to your life-support bridge or tie-in point.

faq.q: Will it fit my top-handle saw?
faq.a: Most top-handle saws have a lanyard ring or eyelet at the rear of the handle. If yours does not, add a manufacturer-approved eyelet before using any lanyard.

name: Buckingham Hi-Viz Chainsaw Lanyard with Snap
title: Buckingham Hi-Viz Chainsaw Lanyard with Snap
h1: Buckingham Hi-Viz Chainsaw Lanyard with Snap
meta: The Buckingham hi viz chainsaw lanyard with snap keeps your saw tethered and easy to spot in the canopy. See how it clips on, who it fits, and typical price.
tagline: A high-visibility bungee saw lanyard with a snap end for quick clip-on and off.
summary: The Buckingham hi viz chainsaw lanyard with snap is a bright bungee saw tether that clips straight to your saw's lanyard ring. The color makes it easy to see in the canopy and on the ground, and the snap end lets you swap saws without untying anything.
highlights: Hi-viz color is easy to spot in foliage and on the trailer
Snap end for quick attachment to the saw
Bungee stretch lets you reach without fighting the saw
Pulls the saw back to your side when you let go

p: A saw lanyard spends its life in sawdust and leaves, so a bright color helps you and your ground crew see where the saw is hanging and where the lanyard runs. It also makes the lanyard easier to find in a gear bag at 6 a.m.

The snap end clips directly to the saw's lanyard point. That makes it quick to swap between a top-handle saw and a handsaw or pole saw during the same climb. Make sure the snap closes fully every time and that it is not loaded across the gate.

Inspect the shock cord and the snap before each climb. Retire the lanyard if the bungee is cut, the sheath is torn, or the snap gate sticks or does not return. Compare other chainsaw lanyards if you prefer a steel ring end or a coiled body.
A saw lanyard is not life support and is never a tie-in point. Run your saw to the manufacturer's instructions, wear your PPE, and follow ANSI Z133 for aloft saw work.

faq.q: Is a snap or a ring end better on a saw lanyard?
faq.a: A snap is faster to clip and unclip; a ring is simpler and has no gate to wear. Many climbers use a snap on the saw side and a fixed attachment on the saddle side.

faq.q: Can I lower the saw on this lanyard?
faq.a: No. A saw lanyard is not designed for lowering. Send the saw up and down on a tool line or with your ground crew.

name: Husqvarna Chainsaw Eyelet
title: Husqvarna Chainsaw Eyelet for Saw Lanyards
meta: A Husqvarna chainsaw eyelet gives your saw a solid lanyard attachment point for climbing. Learn what it does, how to check fit, and what it typically costs.
tagline: A replacement lanyard eyelet for Husqvarna saws used aloft.
summary: A Husqvarna chainsaw eyelet is the small ring or loop on the rear of the saw that your saw lanyard clips into. Climbers replace it when it wears thin or add one to a saw that is going to be used in the tree.
highlights: Gives the saw a dedicated lanyard attachment point
Replacement for a worn or missing eyelet
Lets you clip a bungee saw lanyard securely
Inexpensive part worth checking every season
Confirm the part number for your saw model

p: Top-handle saws built for climbers have a lanyard point at the back of the handle. That eyelet takes the snap or ring of your saw lanyard, so the saw hangs from your saddle when you let go of it. Over time, the eyelet wears from the snap rubbing on it, and on older or rental saws it may be missing entirely.
Husqvarna eyelets vary by saw model, so check the parts diagram or part number for your specific saw before ordering. Install it as the service manual describes and make sure the fasteners are tight.

Look at the eyelet when you sharpen the chain. If the ring is grooved, cracked, bent, or loose in the housing, replace it. A worn eyelet is one of the most common reasons a saw ends up on the ground. Pair it with one of the chainsaw lanyards in this section.
A saw lanyard is not life support and is never a tie-in point. Run your saw to the manufacturer's instructions, wear your PPE, and follow ANSI Z133 for aloft saw work.

faq.q: Will a Husqvarna eyelet fit any saw?
faq.a: No. Eyelets are model-specific. Match the part number to your saw's parts list before buying.

faq.q: Can I tie in to the saw eyelet?
faq.a: Never. The eyelet is only for a saw lanyard. It is not a rated anchor and must not be used for any life-support connection.

name: Reecoil Big Boss Chainsaw Lanyard
title: Reecoil Big Boss Chainsaw Lanyard
meta: The Reecoil Big Boss chainsaw lanyard is a retractable saw tether for heavier saws aloft. See how the reel works, who it suits, and what it typically costs.
tagline: A retractable reel-style saw lanyard sized for heavier saws in the tree.
summary: The Reecoil Big Boss chainsaw lanyard is a retractable saw tether that reels the saw back to your hip instead of using a stretchy bungee. It is the larger version in the Reecoil line, meant for climbers carrying heavier saws aloft.
highlights: Retractable reel keeps slack off your legs
Sized for heavier saws than the standard model
Saw returns to your side when you let go
Clips to a saddle tool ring
specs: Tethering a saw to a climbing saddle

p: A bungee lanyard pulls harder the farther you stretch it, which you feel on a long reach. A retractable reel keeps tension more even and stores the line inside the housing, so there is less loose cord hanging around your legs and lanyard. Many climbers like that it keeps the saw tucked in when moving around the canopy.
The Big Boss is aimed at bigger saws. Check the manufacturer's weight rating against your saw with bar, chain, and a full tank before you choose it, and use the lighter model for small top-handles.

Mount the reel on a tool attachment point on your saddle, not on a life-support ring. Keep sawdust and sap out of the housing, check the line for cuts, and retire it if the retraction gets weak or jerky. You can compare bungee and coiled chainsaw lanyards in this section.
A saw lanyard is not life support and is never a tie-in point. Run your saw to the manufacturer's instructions, wear your PPE, and follow ANSI Z133 for aloft saw work.

faq.q: What is the difference between Reecoil models?
faq.a: The Big Boss is the larger model built for heavier saws. Check the current manufacturer weight ratings to match the lanyard to your saw.

faq.q: Does a retractable lanyard replace a bungee lanyard?
faq.a: It does the same job: it keeps the saw attached and close. Which one you use is mostly about preference and saw weight.

name: Weaver Coil Bungee Chainsaw Lanyard
title: Weaver Coil Bungee Chainsaw Lanyard
meta: The Weaver coil bungee chainsaw lanyard keeps your saw tethered without long loose cord. See how a coiled saw lanyard works aloft and what it typically costs.
tagline: A coiled bungee saw tether that stays compact and out of the way.
summary: The Weaver chainsaw lanyard in coiled bungee form keeps a saw attached to your saddle while you climb. The coil stays short when the saw hangs and stretches out when you raise it to cut.
highlights: Coiled design stays compact at rest
Stretches out for a full reach
Less loose cord to snag on limbs
Clips between saddle tool ring and saw
specs: Tethering a saw to a climbing saddle

p: A straight bungee lanyard can hang in a loop that catches on stubs and your own lanyard. A coiled lanyard pulls itself back into a tight spring when the saw is hanging, so there is less cord flopping around. It still stretches far enough to reach a cut overhead or out on a limb.

Connect the saddle end to a tool ring and the saw end to the saw's lanyard eyelet with a closed connector or the supplied hardware. Check that the saw cannot hang low enough to contact your legs, lanyard, or climbing line.

Coils can tangle if stored loose. Hang the lanyard or clip it short when it goes in the gear bag. Retire it when the coil loses its spring or the cord is cut or abraded. More options are in our chainsaw lanyards section.
A saw lanyard is not life support and is never a tie-in point. Run your saw to the manufacturer's instructions, wear your PPE, and follow ANSI Z133 for aloft saw work.

faq.q: Is a coil lanyard better than a straight bungee?
faq.a: It is mostly preference. Coils stay tidier at rest; straight bungees are simpler and easier to inspect.

faq.q: How long does a coil saw lanyard last?
faq.a: It depends on use and saw weight. Replace it when it no longer pulls the saw back in firmly or the cord shows damage.

name: Weaver Interchangeable Bungee Chainsaw Lanyard
title: Weaver Interchangeable Bungee Chainsaw Lanyard
meta: The Weaver bungee chainsaw lanyard with interchangeable ends lets you move it between saws and saddles. See how it rigs, who it suits, and what it typically costs.
tagline: A bungee saw lanyard built to move between saws and saddles.
summary: The Weaver bungee chainsaw lanyard in the interchangeable style is made to switch between tools or saddles quickly. It gives you the familiar bungee stretch with ends that are easy to swap when you change saws mid-job.
highlights: Interchangeable setup for moving between saws
Bungee stretch for reach, pull-back when you let go
Keeps the saw off the ground crew
Handy for crews sharing saddles or saws
specs: Tethering a saw to a climbing saddle

p: On many jobs you will go up with a top-handle saw, then switch to a handsaw or pole saw, or send the saw down for fuel. An interchangeable lanyard makes that quicker: you unclip the end, swap the tool, and keep working. It is also handy for crews where saddles and saws move between climbers.
Make sure the connectors you use close fully and are not loaded across the gate. Set the length so a hanging saw stays clear of your legs and life-support lines.

Inspect the bungee and ends before each climb. Replace the lanyard if the shock cord is cut, stretched out, or contaminated with fuel. You can compare coiled, hi-viz, and retractable chainsaw lanyards in this section.
A saw lanyard is not life support and is never a tie-in point. Run your saw to the manufacturer's instructions, wear your PPE, and follow ANSI Z133 for aloft saw work.

faq.q: Can I use one lanyard for my saw and handsaw?
faq.a: Yes, that is a common use for an interchangeable lanyard, as long as each tool has a suitable attachment point.

faq.q: Does the bungee lose stretch over time?
faq.a: Yes. Shock cord slowly loses elasticity, especially with sun and fuel exposure. Replace it when it sags.

name: Safety Blue Hi-Vee Adjustable Buckstrap
title: Safety Blue Hi-Vee Adjustable Buckstrap Lanyard
meta: This adjustable buckstrap uses Safety Blue Hi-Vee rope for work positioning around a stem. See how it adjusts, where it fits on the job, and typical price.
tagline: A rope buckstrap-style positioning lanyard made from Safety Blue Hi-Vee.
summary: This adjustable buckstrap is a rope positioning lanyard made from Safety Blue Hi-Vee, a long-running arborist rope. It wraps the stem and adjusts to length so you can lean back and work with both hands.
highlights: Made from Safety Blue Hi-Vee rope
Good for spur work and removals
Easy to inspect braided rope body

p: A buckstrap is an old name for a positioning lanyard that goes around the trunk and clips back to both side D-rings of your saddle. Once adjusted, you lean into it and have both hands free to cut. It is common on spur removals and was the standard setup long before modern rope-grab adjusters.

Safety Blue Hi-Vee is a familiar braided arborist rope with a firm hand, so it holds its shape around the stem and is easy to flip up. Adjust the length so you are close enough to work comfortably but not jammed against the trunk.

A rope buckstrap has no cut-resistant core. If you are working near a running saw, consider a wire-core flipline and always keep a second point of attachment when you cut near your lanyard. Compare other fliplines and lanyards before you choose.
Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: What is a buckstrap?
faq.a: It is a traditional term for an adjustable positioning lanyard that wraps the trunk and connects to both side D-rings of a climbing saddle.

faq.q: Is a rope buckstrap safe to use with a chainsaw?
faq.a: A rope lanyard can be cut by a saw. Many climbers choose a steel-core flipline for removals and always keep a second attachment when cutting near the lanyard.

name: 1/2" Steel Core Positioning Lanyard Prusik Adjuster Kit
title: 1/2" Steel Core Positioning Lanyard Kit with Prusik
h1: 1/2" Steel Core Positioning Lanyard Prusik Adjuster Kit
meta: A 1/2 inch steel core positioning lanyard kit with a prusik adjuster for spur work and removals. See what is in the kit, how it adjusts, and what it typically costs.
tagline: A wire-core flipline with a prusik adjuster for removals and spur climbing.
summary: This steel core positioning lanyard kit pairs a 1/2 inch wire-core flipline with a prusik-style adjuster. The steel core gives cut resistance when you are working close to a running saw on removals.
highlights: Prusik adjuster for quick length changes
Pairs with spurs and a work-positioning saddle
Kit format so the parts are matched

p: On spur removals you are often cutting at or near your own flipline. A wire-core lanyard resists a saw much better than a plain rope lanyard. It is not saw-proof, but it buys you a margin when a cut goes wrong. The prusik adjuster lets you take up or let out length with one hand as the stem tapers.
Steel-core lines are heavier and stiffer than all-rope lanyards. Most climbers keep one for removals and use a lighter rope lanyard for pruning and limb walks.

Tie or attach the prusik as the instructions show and test the grip at ground level before you go up. Inspect the cover for cuts that expose wire, kinks, and crushed sections, and replace the hitch cord when it glazes or fuzzes. More options are in our lanyard kits.

Wire-core lanyards conduct electricity, so never use one near energized lines. Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Is a steel core lanyard chainsaw proof?
faq.a: No. It is more resistant to a saw than an all-rope lanyard, but it can still be cut. Always keep a second attachment when cutting near your lanyard.

faq.q: Can I use a steel core lanyard near power lines?
faq.a: No. The wire core is conductive. Follow ANSI Z133 minimum approach distances and use only qualified line-clearance practices near energized conductors.

name: 2-in-1 Hi-Vee Lanyard Kit
title: 2-in-1 Hi-Vee Lanyard Kit
meta: The 2-in-1 Hi-Vee lanyard kit is a rope positioning lanyard with an adjuster for pruning and spur work. See what it does, who it suits, and what it typically costs.
tagline: An all-rope positioning lanyard kit in Hi-Vee for everyday tree work.
summary: The 2-in-1 Hi-Vee lanyard kit is an all-rope positioning lanyard built around Hi-Vee braided climbing rope, set up so one lanyard covers more than one job. It is a straightforward, familiar kit for climbers who want a rope flipline that is easy to adjust and inspect.
highlights: Lighter and more flexible than wire core
Suited to pruning, limb walks, and spur work
Matched kit, ready to set up

p: A positioning lanyard gives you a second point of attachment and lets you lean back to work with both hands. The 2-in-1 setup is meant to give one lanyard more than one way to work, so you can run it around a stem on spurs or use it as a secondary attachment while pruning. Check the instructions that ship with the kit for the exact configurations it supports.
Hi-Vee has a firm braided hand that holds its shape for flipping and grips well in a friction hitch or adjuster.

Set up the adjuster and test it at ground level. Inspect the rope for cuts, glazing, and stiff spots each time, and retire it after saw contact. For removals, consider a wire-core lanyard. Compare other lanyard kits here.
Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: What does 2-in-1 mean on a lanyard?
faq.a: It refers to a lanyard set up for more than one use. Follow the instructions supplied with the kit for the configurations it is designed and rated for.

faq.q: Is an all-rope lanyard OK for removals?
faq.a: It works, but a rope lanyard can be cut by a saw. Many climbers use a steel-core flipline for removals.

name: Petzl Microflip Wire Core Lanyard Kit
title: Petzl Microflip Wire Core Lanyard Kit
h1: Petzl Microflip Wire Core Lanyard Kit
meta: The Petzl Microflip is a wire core positioning lanyard with a built-in adjuster for spur work and removals. See how it works, who it suits, and typical price.
tagline: A steel-core adjustable flipline with an integrated adjuster for removal climbers.
summary: The Petzl Microflip is a wire core positioning lanyard kit with an integrated mechanical adjuster, aimed at climbers doing spur work and removals. The steel core adds cut resistance and the adjuster lets you change length with one hand.
highlights: Steel-core lanyard rope for cut resistance
One-handed adjustment as the stem tapers

p: The Microflip combines a wire-core lanyard with a dedicated adjuster, so you take up slack by pulling the tail and let it out by working the handle. On a removal you change your lanyard length constantly as the trunk narrows, and a smooth adjuster saves a lot of fumbling with a hitch.
Choose the length based on the trees you climb. A longer lanyard wraps big stems but leaves more tail to manage on small ones.

Check the sheath for cuts exposing wire, kinks, and crushed spots, and inspect the adjuster for wear and smooth action. The wire core is conductive, so this is not a lanyard for work near energized lines. Compare other lanyard kits if you need an all-rope option.
Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: What lengths does the Petzl Microflip come in?
faq.a: It is offered in several lengths, including 2.5, 3.5, 4.5 and 5.5 m. Check current listings for what is in stock.

faq.q: Can the Microflip be cut by a chainsaw?
faq.a: Yes. The steel core improves cut resistance but does not make it saw-proof. Keep a second attachment when cutting near your lanyard.

name: Sterling TriTech Lanyard Kit
title: Sterling TriTech Lanyard Kit
meta: The Sterling TriTech lanyard kit is an all-rope positioning lanyard for pruning and spur work. See how it sets up, who it suits, and what it typically costs.
tagline: An all-rope Sterling positioning lanyard kit for everyday climbing work.
summary: The Sterling TriTech lanyard kit is a ready-to-set-up positioning lanyard built from Sterling's TriTech rope. It gives you a second point of attachment for pruning, limb walks, and spur work without the weight of a wire core.
highlights: Built on Sterling TriTech lanyard rope
Works for pruning and spur work

p: An all-rope lanyard is the everyday choice for many climbers. It is lighter, softer to handle, and easier on bark than a wire core. In a kit, the rope, connectors, and adjuster are matched, so you are not guessing at hitch cord diameter or snap fit.
Use it as your secondary attachment while pruning, around the stem on spur work, or to hold position on a limb walk while you set a cut.

Assemble and test the adjuster at ground level. Inspect the rope for cuts, glazing, and hard spots, and check every connector gate. Retire any lanyard that has touched a running chain. See other lanyard kits if you need wire core or a mechanical adjuster.
Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: What is included in the Sterling TriTech lanyard kit?
faq.a: Kit contents vary by listing. Typically you get the lanyard rope with terminations and an adjuster. Check the listing for connectors and length.

faq.q: Is TriTech good for removals?
faq.a: It is an all-rope lanyard, so it can be cut by a saw. For heavy removal work many climbers prefer steel core.

name: Sterling TriTech Lanyard with ART Positioner
keyword: sterling tritech lanyard with art positioner
title: Sterling TriTech Lanyard with ART Positioner
h1: Sterling TriTech Lanyard with ART Positioner
meta: The Sterling TriTech lanyard with ART Positioner pairs an all-rope flipline with a mechanical adjuster. See how it works, who it suits, and typical price.
tagline: A Sterling rope lanyard paired with the ART Positioner mechanical adjuster.
summary: The Sterling TriTech lanyard with ART Positioner pairs Sterling's lanyard rope with ART's mechanical lanyard adjuster. It gives you smooth one-handed length changes without tending a friction hitch.
highlights: No hitch cord to tend or replace
Good for spur work and long pruning days

p: A prusik or other friction hitch works, but it needs dressing, wears out, and can bind when you are leaning hard. The ART Positioner is a mechanical lanyard adjuster built to grab under load and release smoothly when you want more length. On a long day of spur work or limb walking, that consistency adds up.
Pairing it with a rope made for it matters. Mechanical adjusters are designed around specific rope diameters, and this setup takes the guesswork out of that.

Check the Positioner's moving parts for wear, debris, and sharp edges, and look over the rope for cuts and glazing. Follow ART's instructions for compatible ropes if you ever replace the lanyard. Compare other lanyard kits in this section.
Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Can I use the ART Positioner with any lanyard rope?
faq.a: Only with ropes the manufacturer lists as compatible. Mechanical adjusters depend on rope diameter and construction.

faq.q: Is a mechanical adjuster better than a prusik?
faq.a: It is smoother and needs less tending. A prusik is lighter and cheaper. Both work when set up and inspected properly.

name: Sterling TriTech Positioning Lanyard Kit with Prusik Adjuster
title: Sterling TriTech Positioning Lanyard with Prusik
h1: Sterling TriTech Positioning Lanyard Kit with Prusik Adjuster
meta: The Sterling TriTech positioning lanyard kit with a prusik adjuster is a light all-rope flipline for daily tree work. See setup tips, uses, and typical price.
tagline: An all-rope Sterling flipline with a classic prusik adjuster.
summary: The Sterling TriTech positioning lanyard kit with prusik adjuster is a light all-rope flipline that adjusts with a friction hitch. It is a simple, proven setup that many climbers learn on and keep using.
highlights: Hitch cord is cheap to replace

p: A prusik adjuster is a loop of hitch cord tied around the lanyard rope and clipped to your saddle. Load it and it grips; break it free and it slides. It is light, has no moving parts, and the cord is inexpensive to replace when it wears.
This kit works well as the everyday lanyard for pruning and spur climbing. It is a good choice for newer climbers learning how to manage a flipline.

Dress the hitch neatly and test it at ground level. Replace the hitch cord when it glazes, fuzzes, or slips. Inspect the lanyard rope for cuts and stiff spots. Browse other lanyard kits if you want wire core or a mechanical adjuster.
Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: How often should I replace the prusik on my lanyard?
faq.a: Replace it whenever it shows glazing, cuts, heavy fuzzing, or starts slipping. Hitch cord wears faster than the lanyard rope.

faq.q: Is this lanyard good for beginners?
faq.a: Yes. A prusik-adjusted all-rope lanyard is simple to understand and inspect, which makes it a common first lanyard.

name: Yale Imori Lanyard Kit with Rope Grab
title: Yale Imori Lanyard Kit with Rope Grab
h1: Yale Imori Lanyard Kit with Rope Grab
meta: The Yale Imori lanyard kit with rope grab is an all-rope positioning lanyard with a mechanical adjuster. See how it works, who it suits, and typical price.
tagline: A Yale rope positioning lanyard with a mechanical rope grab adjuster.
summary: The Yale Imori lanyard kit with rope grab combines Yale's Imori rope with a mechanical rope grab for length adjustment. It suits climbers who want a rope lanyard that adjusts quickly without a friction hitch.

p: A rope grab clamps the lanyard under load and slides when you unweight it and move it. Compared to a friction hitch it is quicker to adjust and behaves the same way every time, which is handy when you are repositioning all day.
Yale's Imori is used as the lanyard rope here, and the kit format means the grab and rope are matched for diameter.

Check the rope grab cam and teeth for wear and debris and confirm it locks firmly on the rope before you lean back. Inspect the rope for cuts, glazing, and sheath damage. Rope grabs with teeth can wear a lanyard faster in one spot, so look closely there. See other lanyard kits.
Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Can I swap a different rope into the rope grab?
faq.a: Only ropes the grab's manufacturer lists as compatible. Rope grabs depend on rope diameter and construction.

faq.q: Is a rope grab adjuster better than a prusik?
faq.a: It is faster and more consistent. A prusik is lighter and cheaper. Both are common on positioning lanyards.

name: Yale KernMaster Safari ART Positioner Kit
title: Yale KernMaster Safari ART Positioner Lanyard Kit
h1: Yale KernMaster Safari ART Positioner Kit

summary: The Yale Safari ART Positioner kit pairs Yale lanyard rope with ART's mechanical Positioner adjuster. It is built for climbers who adjust their lanyard all day and want it to feed smoothly without tending a hitch.
highlights: Yale lanyard rope sized for the adjuster
Good for spur work and pruning

p: This kit sets a Yale lanyard rope up with the ART Positioner, a mechanical lanyard adjuster. The Positioner grabs when you load it and lets rope through smoothly when you want more length, so you can make small changes while leaning back on a stem.
A kit is the easy way to get a mechanical adjuster running on a rope the manufacturer intends it for, rather than building one from parts.

Keep sawdust and sap out of the Positioner and check its moving parts and contact surfaces for wear. Inspect the rope over its full length, especially where the adjuster rides. Compare other lanyard kits if you want a simpler prusik setup.
Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Why buy the kit instead of parts?
faq.a: A kit pairs the adjuster with a rope intended for it, so you are not guessing at diameter or compatibility.

faq.q: Does the ART Positioner need special care?
faq.a: Keep it clean, inspect it before each use, and follow ART's instructions for maintenance and rope compatibility.

name: Yale R.I.N.G. Lanyard Kit with Triple Locking Snap
title: Yale R.I.N.G. Lanyard Kit with Triple Locking Snap
h1: Yale R.I.N.G. Lanyard Kit with Triple Locking Snap
meta: The Yale R.I.N.G. lanyard kit with a triple locking snap is a rope positioning lanyard for pruning and spur work. See setup notes, uses, and typical price.
tagline: A Yale rope positioning lanyard kit finished with a triple-locking snap.
summary: The Yale R.I.N.G. lanyard kit with triple locking snap is an all-rope positioning lanyard built on Yale's R.I.N.G. rope and finished with a triple-action snap. The snap gives a secure gate when clipping to your saddle D-rings.
highlights: All-rope body, lighter than wire core
For pruning, limb walks, and spur work

p: A triple-locking snap needs three separate actions to open, which makes accidental gate opening very unlikely when the snap rubs against bark, branches, or other gear. It also clips cleanly to a saddle D-ring without the cross-loading risk that a carabiner can have.
Paired with an all-rope lanyard, it makes a light, secure positioning setup for everyday climbing.

Check the snap gate for full closure and smooth return, and look for wear on the eye where the rope is attached. Inspect the rope for cuts, glazing, and hard spots. See other lanyard kits in this section.
Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: What is a triple-locking snap?
faq.a: A snap hook that needs three separate motions to open the gate, which reduces the chance of it opening by accident.

faq.q: Can I clip a snap to any saddle ring?
faq.a: Clip it to the D-rings the saddle maker designates for positioning lanyards, and make sure the snap is compatible with the ring's size and shape.

name: Yale R.I.N.G. Lanyard Kit
title: Yale R.I.N.G. Lanyard Kit
meta: The Yale R.I.N.G. lanyard kit is an all-rope positioning lanyard ready to set up for pruning and spur work. See how it adjusts, who it suits, and typical price.
tagline: An all-rope Yale positioning lanyard kit for everyday climbing.
summary: The Yale R.I.N.G. lanyard kit is an all-rope positioning lanyard built on Yale's R.I.N.G. rope. It is a straightforward secondary attachment for pruning, limb walking, and spur work.
highlights: Lighter and softer than wire core

p: Most climbers keep a light rope lanyard on the saddle for every climb. It lets you hold position on a limb while you set a cut, gives you a second attachment when you are cutting, and wraps the stem when you are on spurs.
A kit puts the rope and adjuster together so the diameters match. That matters because a friction hitch or rope grab behaves differently on a rope it was not meant for.

Test the adjuster at ground level, inspect the rope before every climb, and retire it after any saw contact. If you want a snap with an extra lock, look at the triple-locking version in our lanyard kits.
Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: What length lanyard should I get?
faq.a: Pick a length that wraps the largest stems you climb with some tail to spare. Longer lanyards leave more tail to manage on small trees.

faq.q: How do I know when to retire a lanyard?
faq.a: Retire it after cuts, saw contact, glazing, crushed spots, or chemical exposure, or when the manufacturer's service life is reached.

name: Yale Safari Lanyard Kit
title: Yale Safari Lanyard Kit
meta: The Yale Safari lanyard kit is an all-rope positioning lanyard for pruning, limb walks, and spur work. See how it sets up, who it suits, and what it typically costs.
tagline: A Yale rope positioning lanyard kit for daily climbing work.
summary: The Yale Safari lanyard kit is an all-rope positioning lanyard set up and ready to adjust. It gives you a reliable second attachment for pruning, limb walks, and spur climbing.
highlights: Works for pruning and spur work

p: The positioning lanyard is the second tool you reach for after your climbing line. You use it to hold yourself in place while you set up a cut, to keep two points of attachment when you are cutting, and to wrap the trunk when you are on spurs.
An all-rope lanyard like this one is light and easy on your hands, and it is simple to inspect. Save wire core for heavy removal days.

Inspect the full length of rope before each climb and check the adjuster and connectors. Retire it after any saw contact. If you want a mechanical adjuster, see the ART Positioner versions in our lanyard kits.
Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Is the Yale Safari lanyard good for spur work?
faq.a: Yes, for general spur climbing. For heavy removals near a running saw, many climbers choose a steel-core flipline.

faq.q: Can I replace just the lanyard rope?
faq.a: Yes, as long as the replacement is compatible with your adjuster. Replacement rope lanyards are also available.

name: Aluminum Prusik Snap Lanyard Adjuster
title: Aluminum Prusik Snap Lanyard Adjuster
meta: An aluminum prusik snap lanyard adjuster connects a friction hitch on your flipline to your saddle. Learn how it works, what to check, and what it typically costs.
tagline: A lightweight snap for running a prusik-style adjuster on your lanyard.
summary: An aluminum prusik snap lanyard adjuster is a snap hook used to connect a prusik or other friction hitch on your positioning lanyard to your saddle. The aluminum body keeps weight down compared with a steel snap.
highlights: Connects a lanyard hitch to the saddle D-ring
Lets you adjust lanyard length on the fly
Simple, no moving cam parts on the rope
specs: Snap hook for prusik lanyard adjuster

p: With a prusik-style adjuster, a loop of hitch cord is tied around the lanyard rope and clipped to a snap that goes on your saddle D-ring. Load it and the hitch grips; push it along and it slides. The snap is the link between that hitch and your saddle, so it needs a secure gate and a smooth eye for the cord to sit in.
Aluminum keeps it light, which you notice when you are carrying a full rack all day.

Check the gate closes and locks fully, and look for grooves or sharp edges where the hitch cord bears. Aluminum wears faster than steel under rope, so retire it if it develops a groove. Replace the hitch cord when it glazes. Compare mechanical options in rope grabs.
Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Do I need a special snap for a prusik adjuster?
faq.a: You need a rated, locking connector that suits your saddle ring and holds the hitch cord without pinching it. A dedicated prusik snap is designed for that.

faq.q: Aluminum or steel snap?
faq.a: Aluminum is lighter; steel resists wear better. Either works when it is rated and inspected.

name: 2-in-1 Blaze Replacement Lanyard
title: 2-in-1 Blaze Replacement Lanyard
meta: The 2-in-1 Blaze replacement lanyard swaps a worn rope into your existing adjuster and snaps. See what to check before ordering and what it typically costs today.
tagline: A replacement lanyard rope in Blaze for refreshing a worn 2-in-1 setup.
summary: The 2-in-1 Blaze replacement lanyard is a replacement rope for a 2-in-1 style positioning lanyard, made in Blaze climbing rope. It lets you retire a worn lanyard rope while keeping hardware that is still in good shape.
highlights: Keep hardware that still passes inspection
Bright color is easy to see aloft
Cheaper than buying a full kit

p: Lanyard rope wears faster than the snaps and adjuster on it. It gets flipped around bark, rubbed on spurs, and sometimes nicked by a saw. When the rope is glazed, cut, stiff, or fuzzed, but your connectors and adjuster still pass inspection, a replacement lanyard is the economical fix.
Blaze is a bright, firm arborist rope that is easy to spot and flip around a stem.

Match the replacement to your existing adjuster and terminations so the hitch or grab works as intended. Inspect every hardware piece you plan to reuse, and retire anything with wear or a sticky gate. See other rope lanyards in this section.
Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Can I reuse my old snaps on a new lanyard?
faq.a: Only if they pass inspection and are compatible with the new rope and terminations. When in doubt, replace them.

faq.q: Will this fit my existing adjuster?
faq.a: Check the rope diameter and the adjuster maker's compatibility list before ordering.

name: Assorted Rope Lanyard
title: Assorted Rope Lanyard for Tree Climbing
meta: An assorted rope lanyard is a budget positioning lanyard made from mixed arborist rope. See what you get, how to check it before use, and what it typically costs.
tagline: A budget-friendly rope lanyard made from assorted arborist rope.
summary: An assorted rope lanyard is a positioning lanyard made from whatever arborist rope is on hand, so color and rope type vary. It is a low-cost way to get a spare or backup rope lanyard for the truck.
highlights: Good spare for the truck or a new climber
Check the tag for rope details

p: Assorted lanyards are made from mixed arborist rope, so the color, brand, and construction can vary from one to the next. It is a good way to get a working rope lanyard for less money, especially as a backup or as a lanyard for a new crew member.
Because the rope varies, check the tag and confirm the diameter suits your adjuster before you set it up.

Inspect the rope over its full length, check terminations and any connectors, and test your adjuster at ground level. Retire it after saw contact, cuts, or glazing. For a specific rope, see the other rope lanyards here.
Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Can I pick the color of an assorted lanyard?
faq.a: Usually not. Assorted means rope type and color vary by what is available.

faq.q: Is an assorted lanyard safe to climb on?
faq.a: It is safe when it meets the applicable standard, is in good condition, and is set up with a compatible adjuster. Inspect it before every climb.

name: K1 Keeper by Teufelberger
title: Teufelberger K1 Keeper for Rope Lanyards
meta: The Teufelberger K1 Keeper is a small accessory for rope lanyard setups. See what it does, how to check fit with your lanyard, and what it typically costs.
tagline: A small Teufelberger accessory for keeping a rope lanyard setup in order.
summary: The Teufelberger K1 Keeper is a small accessory sold for rope lanyard setups, used to keep parts of the lanyard in place. It is a minor part, but it helps keep your lanyard tidy and working the way it was set up.
highlights: Helps keep the lanyard setup in position
Check compatibility with your rope diameter

p: Keepers on a lanyard hold a hitch, termination, or connector in its intended position so it does not wander, flip, or cross-load when you move around. Small parts like this make a lanyard easier to manage when you are flipping it up a stem or clipping in one-handed.
Check Teufelberger's instructions for the exact use and compatible ropes before fitting it. A keeper is not a load-bearing part unless the manufacturer says so.

Fit it as the instructions show and confirm it does not interfere with your adjuster or connector gate. Replace it when it tears, stretches out, or stops holding. Browse complete rope lanyards if your lanyard needs replacing too.
Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Is the K1 Keeper load-bearing?
faq.a: Treat it as a positioning aid, not a load-bearing part, unless Teufelberger's instructions state otherwise.

faq.q: Will it fit my lanyard?
faq.a: Check the manufacturer's rope diameter range against your lanyard rope before buying.

name: Lanyard Management Clips
title: Lanyard Management Clips for Climbing Saddles
meta: Lanyard management clips keep the tail of your flipline stowed on your saddle so it does not snag. See how climbers use them and what they typically cost today.
tagline: Clips that keep lanyard tail stowed and out of the way on your saddle.
summary: Lanyard management clips hold the extra tail of your positioning lanyard on the saddle so it does not hang in loops and catch on limbs, spurs, or your saw. They are a small, cheap fix for a common annoyance.
highlights: Stow excess lanyard tail on the saddle
Keeps loops away from spurs and saw

p: When you adjust a long lanyard short around a small stem, the leftover tail hangs in a loop. That loop catches on stubs, gets stepped on with a spur, or ends up near the bar. A management clip lets you gather the tail and park it on your saddle until you need the length again.
Mount them on gear loops or a saddle accessory bar, out of the way of your bridge and life-support rings.
These clips are for storage only. Never clip a life-support line, a tie-in, or a load into one. Replace them if they crack or stop holding shut. You will find complete rope lanyards in this section.
Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Can I clip my lanyard to these when I lean back?
faq.a: No. They are storage clips only and are not rated for any load.

faq.q: Where should I mount them?
faq.a: On a gear loop or accessory point on your saddle, away from your bridge and life-support connections.

name: Poison Moon Replacement Lanyard
title: Poison Moon Replacement Lanyard
meta: The Poison Moon replacement lanyard lets you swap a worn lanyard rope while keeping hardware that still passes inspection. See what to check and typical price.
tagline: A replacement rope lanyard in Poison Moon for refreshing a worn setup.
summary: The Poison Moon replacement lanyard is a replacement positioning lanyard rope made in Poison Moon climbing line. It is meant for climbers whose lanyard rope is worn but whose adjuster and snaps are still good.
highlights: Replacement for a worn lanyard rope

p: The rope is the part of a positioning lanyard that takes the most abuse. It wraps rough bark, picks up sap and grit, and is the part closest to the saw. Snaps and adjusters often outlast two or three ropes. Replacing only the rope keeps a familiar setup working for less money.
Before ordering, confirm the rope diameter is compatible with your adjuster or hitch cord.

Inspect the new rope and any reused hardware carefully. Retire connectors with grooves, cracks, or sticky gates. Test the adjuster at ground level after setup. Compare other rope lanyards in this section.
Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: How do I know my hardware is still good?
faq.a: Check gates for full closure and smooth return, look for grooves, cracks, and corrosion, and follow the manufacturer's inspection guidance. Replace anything in doubt.

faq.q: Will this rope work with my rope grab?
faq.a: Only if its diameter and construction are on the rope grab maker's compatibility list.

name: Sterling TriTech Lanyard with Triple Locking Snap
title: Sterling TriTech Lanyard with Triple Locking Snap
h1: Sterling TriTech Lanyard with Triple Locking Snap
meta: The Sterling TriTech lanyard with snap uses a triple locking snap for a secure saddle connection. See how it fits your lanyard setup and what it typically costs.
tagline: A Sterling rope lanyard terminated with a triple-locking snap.
summary: The Sterling TriTech lanyard with snap is a rope positioning lanyard terminated with a triple-locking snap hook. Use it as a replacement lanyard rope or build your own setup with the adjuster of your choice.
highlights: Pair with your choice of adjuster
Good replacement for a worn lanyard

p: This is the lanyard rope with a snap on it, without a full kit around it. That makes it a good choice when you already have an adjuster you like, whether a prusik or a mechanical positioner, and only need fresh rope.
The triple-locking snap needs three actions to open, which helps keep it shut when it rubs against bark or other gear.

Confirm your adjuster is compatible with the rope, set it up, and test it at ground level. Inspect the snap gate and rope before every climb. Retire the lanyard after saw contact. See more rope lanyards.
Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Does this include an adjuster?
faq.a: This listing is for the lanyard with a snap. Add a prusik or mechanical adjuster that is compatible with the rope.

faq.q: Why a triple-locking snap instead of a carabiner?
faq.a: Snaps sit naturally on saddle D-rings and resist cross-loading. The triple lock reduces the chance of the gate opening by accident.

name: Yale Spearmint Lanyard with Steel Double Locking Snap
title: Yale Spearmint Lanyard with Steel Snap
h1: Yale Spearmint Lanyard with Steel Double Locking Snap
meta: The Yale Spearmint lanyard with a steel double locking snap is a rope positioning lanyard for tree work. See what it suits, how to set it up, and typical price.
tagline: A Yale Spearmint rope lanyard with a durable steel double-locking snap.
summary: The Yale Spearmint lanyard is a rope positioning lanyard finished with a steel double-locking snap. Steel wears slowly, so the snap holds up well to the rubbing a lanyard end takes on a saddle D-ring.
highlights: Pair with a prusik or mechanical adjuster

p: A steel snap is heavier than aluminum but far more resistant to wear, which matters on a connector that rides on a D-ring all day. The double-locking gate needs two actions to open, a long-standing design for arborist lanyards.
The rope body is light and flexible, easy to flip around a stem, and simple to inspect.

Add a compatible adjuster, test it at ground level, and check the snap closes and locks every time. Inspect the rope for cuts, glazing, and hard spots. Retire it after saw contact. Compare other rope lanyards here.
Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Double-locking or triple-locking snap?
faq.a: Both are used on arborist lanyards. A triple lock adds one more step to open; a double lock is quicker. Follow your company's policy and the manufacturer's instructions.

faq.q: Is steel better than aluminum for a snap?
faq.a: Steel wears more slowly and handles abuse better; aluminum is lighter. For a lanyard end that rubs all day, many climbers prefer steel.

name: ANSI Arborist Crane Tie-In Point with Carabiners
title: Arborist Crane Tie-In Point with Carabiners
h1: ANSI Arborist Crane Tie-In Point with Carabiners
meta: An arborist crane tie in point gives a climber a dedicated connection to the crane hook. See what the kit includes, how it is used, and what it typically costs.
tagline: A crane tie-in assembly with connectors for climbers working off a crane.
summary: An arborist crane tie in point is a dedicated connection that lets a climber attach to a crane hook or load line when being flown into position. This version comes with carabiners, so the assembly arrives ready to inspect and use.
highlights: Dedicated climber connection for crane work
Keeps the climber's attachment separate from the load

p: On crane-assisted removals, the climber is sometimes lifted into the tree or rides the hook to a pick point. ANSI Z133 sets specific requirements for crane-assisted climbing, and the climber's connection should stay independent of the load rigging. A dedicated tie-in point gives a clear, rated attachment on the crane's hook block.
This version includes carabiners, so you have matched connectors for the assembly.

Crane work requires a qualified crane operator, a qualified signal person, and a plan agreed before the lift. Inspect the tie-in point and connectors before every use and retire anything with wear, cuts, or deformation. Compare other anchors in friction savers.
Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Can a climber tie in to the crane hook with a regular lanyard?
faq.a: Follow ANSI Z133, the crane manufacturer, and your company's crane procedures. A dedicated tie-in point keeps the climber's connection clear and inspectable.

faq.q: Who can do crane-assisted tree work?
faq.a: Only trained, qualified climbers working with a qualified crane operator and signal person, under an agreed lift plan.

name: ANSI Arborist Crane Tie-In Point
title: ANSI Arborist Crane Tie-In Point
meta: A crane tie in point gives an arborist a dedicated connection to the crane hook during crane-assisted removals. See how it is used, what to inspect, and price.
tagline: A dedicated climber connection for crane-assisted tree work.
summary: A crane tie in point is a dedicated attachment that lets a climber connect to a crane hook block separately from the load rigging. This version is the assembly without carabiners, for crews that supply their own rated connectors.
highlights: Dedicated climber attachment for crane work
Keeps climber connection separate from the load
Use with your own rated connectors

p: On crane jobs, the climber may ride the hook into the tree or need a secure attachment to the hook block while a pick is rigged. A dedicated tie-in point gives a clear, inspectable connection and helps keep the climber's attachment independent from slings and chokers on the load.
This listing is the tie-in point alone, for crews that already carry the connectors their procedures specify.

Crane-assisted tree work needs a qualified crane operator, a signal person, and an agreed lift plan. Use only rated, compatible locking connectors, and inspect everything before each lift. See also friction savers for tree anchors.
Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: What connectors should I use with it?
faq.a: Use rated, locking connectors that are compatible with the tie-in point and the crane hook, as specified by the manufacturer and your crane procedures.

faq.q: Is this a rigging sling?
faq.a: No. It is for the climber's attachment only. Never use it to rig loads.

name: ART RopeGuide
title: ART RopeGuide Friction Saver
meta: The ART RopeGuide is a canopy rope management device that reduces friction and bark wear at your tie-in. See how it works, who it suits, and what it typically costs.
tagline: A canopy rope guide from ART for smoother running and less bark wear.
summary: The ART RopeGuide is a canopy device that guides your climbing line over a limb, reducing friction and protecting the bark at your anchor or redirect. It is aimed at climbers who want smoother rope travel than a bare branch union gives.
highlights: Guides rope over a limb with less friction
From ART, makers of the Positioner and Spiderjack

body.h: What it does in the canopy
p: Climbing over a bare union wears your rope, damages bark, and adds friction you fight on every advance. A rope guide sits on the limb and gives the rope a smoother path. On a moving rope system that means easier hitch tending, and at a redirect it keeps the line running where you want it.
Read ART's instructions for the setups it is rated for, including whether it is approved as a primary anchor or only as a guide or redirect.

Check all metal parts for grooves, cracks, and sharp edges, and inspect any textile parts for cuts and abrasion. Make sure it is set on a sound limb. Compare cambium savers and other friction savers in this section.
Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Can the ART RopeGuide be used as a primary anchor?
faq.a: Follow ART's instructions. Use it only in the configurations the manufacturer approves for your climbing system.

faq.q: Is it for MRS or SRS?
faq.a: Check the manufacturer's instructions for the systems it is designed for before you set it in the canopy.

name: ART SnakeAnchor
title: ART SnakeAnchor Adjustable Tree Anchor
meta: The ART SnakeAnchor is an adjustable canopy anchor for climbing systems that wraps limbs of different sizes. See how it works, who it suits, and what it typically costs.
tagline: An adjustable ART canopy anchor that wraps limbs of different sizes.
summary: The ART SnakeAnchor is an adjustable canopy anchor that wraps a limb or stem and gives your climbing system a defined attachment point. It is built to handle different limb sizes without carrying several fixed-length slings.
highlights: Gives a defined anchor point in the canopy
Protects bark compared with a bare tie-in
Reduces the need for multiple fixed slings

p: A fixed-length cambium saver or sling only fits a range of limb sizes. An adjustable anchor like the SnakeAnchor can be snugged around whatever union or stem you pick, which helps when the best tie-in is not the size your gear is cut for.
Follow ART's instructions for installation, retrieval, and the climbing systems it is rated for. Choose a sound, appropriately sized limb as you would with any anchor.

Inspect all components before every climb. Look for cuts, abrasion, and stiff spots on textiles, and wear or deformation on metal parts. Retire it after any shock load or damage. Compare other friction savers and anchors in this section.
Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Is the SnakeAnchor retrievable from the ground?
faq.a: Check ART's instructions for the retrieval methods and configurations they approve.

faq.q: Who is the SnakeAnchor for?
faq.a: Trained climbers who want one anchor that adapts to different limb sizes. Newer climbers often start with a simple ring-and-ring friction saver.

name: Buckingham Buck SuperSaver
title: Buckingham Buck SuperSaver Friction Saver
meta: The Buckingham SuperSaver is a friction saver that protects bark and your climbing rope at the tie-in. See how it installs, who it suits, and what it typically costs.
tagline: A Buckingham friction saver that protects the tree and your climbing line.
summary: The Buckingham SuperSaver is a friction saver that goes over your tie-in limb to protect the bark and keep your climbing rope from wearing on the union. It gives your rope a smoother, more consistent path on a doubled-rope system.
highlights: Protects bark and cambium at the tie-in
Simple to install with a throw line

p: On a moving rope system the rope runs back and forth over the tie-in limb every time you advance or descend. Over a bare union, that grinds the bark and wears your rope. A friction saver gives the rope a ring or eye to run through, which protects the tree, extends rope life, and makes the system feel smoother.
Install it with your throw line so the rings or eyes sit correctly over a sound limb, and follow Buckingham's instructions for retrieval.

Check the strap or rope body for cuts and abrasion, and look at the rings or hardware for grooves and wear. Retire it if it shows damage or has been shock loaded. Compare other friction savers in this section.
Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Does a friction saver help on SRS?
faq.a: It can serve as an anchor in some SRS setups. Follow the manufacturer's instructions for the configurations it is approved for.

faq.q: How do I get a friction saver out of the tree?
faq.a: Most are retrieved from the ground by pulling the rope through in the order shown in the instructions. Practice low before you rely on it in a big tree.
